catalog_quote: Stress usually falls on the first syllable of a group of morphemes joining together and forming what can conveniently be called a "word" in Atʸnʸamat̯an̯a. Stress is not marked, neither is secondary stress, which tends to fall on the penultimate syllable of a word. [p. xvi] ... The criterion for considering an element a clitic or a particle respectively is stress: the clitics influence the position of the secondary stress of the word to which they are added - just as the other suffixes in the language do - while the particles do not. Thus, for instance, án̯aŋa 'there' has no noticeable secondary stress, while ⁺án̯aŋàku 'but there, there however' does have a secondary stress on the penultimate syllable. On the other hand in ⁺án̯aŋa utʸu 'there + emphasis', the first element án̯aŋa 'there' does not show any change in the stress pattern, while the emphatic particle utʸu (see p. 38) is normally unstressed; this particle therefore behaves like an "enclitic". Other particles clearly behave as independent words do in that they have a primary stress; for example nímpatʸi 'like this' and nímpatʸìn̯a 'like this' + the suffix -n̯a. [p. 35] ... the pronoun is stressed and the particle always unstressed ("enclitic" in the traditional sense) [p. 38] ... the few examples which are considered such have only one main stress. [p. 50] ... Stress always falls on the first syllable of a word and is not marked. [Schebeck 1973, note 2, p. 29]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (Schebeck 1974, PL D-21, sealang CRCL CC BY-SA online edition, 298 pp., text layer present). PDF p.16 = book p. xvi 'NOTES ON TRANSCRIPTION' ends with exactly the quoted sentence: 'Stress usually falls on the first syllable of a group of morphemes joining together and forming what can conveniently be called a "word" in AtYnYamatana. Stress is not marked, neither is secondary stress, which tends to fall on the penultimate syllable of a word.' (verbatim apart from text-layer letter-spacing). Supporting passages also verified at the stated locators: p.30 (PDF p.50) '-wa.. is always preceded by a syllable containing the secondary stress'; p.35 (PDF p.55) sect. 3 Clitics and Particles: 'T…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable of the phonological word (stem plus its suffixes/clitics); a secondary stress tends to fall on the penultimate syllable of that word, and moves rightward when suffixes or clitics are added (free particles do not affect it). Schebeck 1973 (PL A-36 p. 29) states it more flatly: 'Stress always falls on the first syllable of a word.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress tends to fall on the penult of the word; suffixes and clitics shift it to the new penult (diagnostic for clitic vs particle, p. 35); 3sg -wa is always preceded by a secondary-stressed syllable (p. 30); clitic -naya carries secondary stress on its first syllable (p. 36).
new_statements.exceptions: 'usually' (hedged); emphatic particle utʸu is normally unstressed and behaves like an enclitic; other particles (e.g. nimpatʸi 'like this') carry their own primary stress; compounds have a single main stress (p. 50); vowels (esp. a) may be elided in rapid speech.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'word' defined as a group of morphemes joined together (stem + suffixes + clitics); description based on texts dictated by Andrew Coulthard (Nepabunna, Flinders Ranges), impressionistic, no acoustic measurement.
new_statements.identity_note: Schebeck's 'Atʸnʸamat̯an̯a' / 'Adnjamathanha' = Adnyamathanha (adny1235), speech of Andrew Coulthard and others at Nepabunna, northern Flinders Ranges; Schebeck and Hercus treat Adnyamathanha and Kuyani (Guyani) as dialects of one language, but the texts and notes are Adnyamathanha proper.

sources.note: p. xvi (Notes on Transcription): stress usually falls on the first syllable of the (phonological) word; secondary stress tends to fall on the penultimate syllable. Grammatical notes add: 3sg suffix -wa is always preceded by a secondary-stressed syllable (p.30); clitics vs particles are distinguished by whether they shift the host's secondary stress to the new penult, e.g. aŋaŋa 'there' vs aŋaŋa-ku with secondary stress on penult (p.35); clitic -naya always has (secondary) stress on its first syllable (p.36); compounds have only one main stress (p.50).
